Part 1

Precipitation as an atmospheric process

The forms precipitation takes, and the energy and temperature structure behind them

Types of precipitation

Key idea

Precipitation is classified by the size and state of what falls: from fine drizzle to hailstones up to 125 mm across.

Liquid

  • Drizzle: fine droplets 0.1–0.5 mm, close together
  • Rain: drops 0.5–0.7 mm or larger
  • Freezing rain or drizzle: freezes on impact with a solid surface

Solid or mixed

  • Sleet: partly melted snow, or rain and snow together (UK); ice pellets (USA)
  • Snow: ice crystals, single or as snowflakes
  • Snow grains, snow pellets (graupel), ice pellets
  • Hail: balls of ice 5–125 mm, often in concentric layers

Precipitation as an atmospheric process

Key idea

The vertical temperature and moisture profile of the atmosphere decides whether snow, sleet, freezing rain or rain reaches the ground.

Energy and water vapor

  • Evaporation requires energy input; condensation releases energy
  • Water is in the air: the maximum amount of water vapor depends on air temperature
  • Dust provides condensation nuclei, sites where vapor condenses or deposits into cloud droplets, ice or rain

Read the four panels

  • (a) Snow: deep cold layer all the way down
  • (b) Melting/wet snow: a thin warm layer near the surface
  • (c) Ice pellets: a shallow warm layer aloft, so snow melts then refreezes
  • (d) Freezing rain: a deep warm layer, then a thin cold layer at the surface

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 What is the difference between sleet (ice pellets) and freezing rain?

Ice pellets refreeze in the air after passing through a shallow warm layer. Freezing rain falls as liquid through a deep warm layer and freezes on impact with a cold surface.

Q2 Why does the atmosphere need dust to make rain?

Dust and other particles act as condensation nuclei: surfaces on which water vapor can condense or deposit to form droplets or ice.

Part 2

Water vapor in the air

Vapor pressure, saturation, dew point, humidity and vapor pressure deficit

Atmospheric pressure and vapor pressure

Key idea

A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the atmospheric pressure around it.

Read the left figure

  • Evaporation: bubbles cannot form, because the vapor pressure is less than atmospheric pressure
  • Boiling: bubbles form and rise, because the vapor pressure overcomes atmospheric pressure

Read the right figure

A closed container: molecules leave and return to the liquid at the same rate. The vapor is saturated, and its pressure (often in mmHg) is the saturated vapor pressure.

Vapor pressure

Key idea

Vapor pressure is the part of total atmospheric pressure that is due to water vapor (its partial pressure).

Units: pascals (Pa) or millibars (mb).

Read the curve

The curve is the saturation vapor pressure, which rises steeply with temperature. Below the curve air is undersaturated; above it, supersaturated.

Evaporation vs. boiling

  • Evaporation: moderate fluid temperature, low vapor pressure. Vapor P < air P, and vapor P < fluid P
  • Boiling: high fluid temperature, high vapor pressure. Vapor P > air P, and vapor P > fluid P

Saturation vapor pressure and dew point

Key idea

Cool air to its dew point and it becomes saturated: water condenses on the nearest cool surface.

Saturation vapor pressure (100% humidity)

The maximum amount of water vapor air can hold before condensation or sublimation. Beyond it, condensation occurs and water droplets form.

Dew point temperature

The temperature that air with its current vapor content would have to be cooled to in order to be saturated.

Everyday examples

  • Water condenses on a bottle that is much cooler than the air around it
  • Morning dew: moisture condenses on surfaces that cooled overnight

Relative humidity (RH)

Key idea

RH = eₐ / eₛ × 100%: actual vapor pressure as a share of saturation vapor pressure at that temperature.

  • eₐ: actual water vapor pressure
  • eₛ: saturation vapor pressure

Read the figure

Each container is air at 50% RH. Warmer air is a bigger container, so it holds more water at the same RH:

  • 55 °F (13 °C) air at 50% RH → dew point 37 °F (2.8 °C)
  • 75 °F (24 °C) → dew point 55 °F (13 °C)
  • 95 °F (35 °C) → dew point 74 °F (23 °C)

Temperature, RH and dew point are all interrelated. A steam room and a rain forest are both near 100% RH.

Types of humidity: important to distinguish

Key idea

Each humidity measure answers a different question: how much vapor, as a share of what, and compared with saturation?

Absolute humidity

Total amount of water vapor in a given volume of air, regardless of temperature.

Specific humidity

Ratio of water vapor mass to the air parcel's total mass.

Relative humidity

Ratio of the partial pressure of water vapor to the saturated vapor pressure at a given temperature.

Mixing ratio

Mass of water vapor relative to the mass of the other gases.

Vapor pressure deficit (VPD)

Key idea

VPD = eₛ − eₐ = eₛ(1 − RH): how far the air is from saturation, expressed as a pressure.

Worked example

At 22 °C and 80% RH:

  • Saturation vapor pressure eₛ = 2.64 kPa
  • Actual vapor pressure eₐ = 0.80 × 2.64 = 2.12 kPa
  • VPD = 2.64 − 2.12 = 0.52 kPa

Read the table

Find the 22 °C row and the 80% column. VPD rises with temperature and falls as RH rises. High VPD means dry air that pulls water out of leaves and soil (Lecture 4e).

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q3 At 22 °C the saturation vapor pressure is 2.64 kPa. If RH is 50%, what are eₐ and the VPD?

eₐ = 0.5 × 2.64 = 1.32 kPa; VPD = 2.64 − 1.32 = 1.32 kPa.

Q4 Two air masses both have 50% RH, one at 13 °C and one at 35 °C. Which holds more water vapor, and which has the higher dew point?

The 35 °C air holds more vapor and has the higher dew point (about 23 °C vs. 2.8 °C).

Q5 Which humidity measure is a ratio of masses of vapor to total air, and which is a ratio of pressures?

Specific humidity compares masses (vapor to total air). Relative humidity compares pressures (actual to saturation).

Part 3

How precipitation forms

Saturation, condensation nuclei, the four lifting mechanisms, and cloud seeding

Precipitation formation

Key idea

Warm, moist air → cooling → condensation → precipitation.

Four conditions

1. The atmosphere becomes saturated:

  • a humid air mass is lifted
  • the air cools as it rises
  • saturation is reached

2. Condensation nuclei are present

3. Water particles collide to form droplets large enough to fall

4. A constant supply of warm, moist air

Four atmospheric lifting mechanisms

Key idea

Lifting makes air rise and cool. With enough moisture and instability, that forms clouds and rain.

Lift is the trigger in step 1 of precipitation formation.

The four mechanisms

  • Convection: surface heating makes air rise
  • Convergence: winds meet at low pressure and are forced up
  • Frontal: one air mass is pushed over another
  • Orographic: mountains force air up

The next four slides take each one in turn; the bar at the bottom shows which.

Convection lifting

  1. Convection
  2. Convergence
  3. Frontal
  4. Orographic
Key idea

A parcel of air next to the warm surface is heated, rises, expands and cools until it condenses into cloud.

  • Lifting is stronger when heating is differential: some areas warm while others stay cool
  • Example: a plowed field heats faster than the surrounding forest, so warm air rises above it
  • Common on sunny summer days near moisture sources such as fields, rivers or lakes

A typical day

It starts clear and sunny, puffy white fair-weather cumulus clouds appear by afternoon, and they dissipate at night.

Convergent lifting

  1. Convection
  2. Convergence
  3. Frontal
  4. Orographic
Key idea

Winds flowing into an area of low surface pressure collide and force air upward.

Best example: the ITCZ

The InterTropical Convergence Zone is a band of low pressure circling Earth near the Equator. It moves north and south with the sun's most intense rays.

What it produces

Consistent, plentiful rainfall, over 100 inches per year in many places, creating the rainforests of the Amazon, Congo and Indonesia.

Frontal lifting

  1. Convection
  2. Convergence
  3. Frontal
  4. Orographic
Key idea

When two air masses meet, the warmer, lighter air is forced up and over the colder, denser air.

  • Common across much of North America
  • Cold front: a colder air mass moves into a warmer one, pushing the warm air up (shown in the figure)
  • Warm fronts and occluded fronts also cause lifting and precipitation

Read the figure

cP (continental polar) cold air wedges under mT (maritime tropical) warm, humid air.

Orographic lifting

  1. Convection
  2. Convergence
  3. Frontal
  4. Orographic
Key idea

Mountains force moving air to rise. Air cools and drops its moisture on the windward side; the leeward side stays dry.

  • Needs a steady wind (a constant supply of new air) and a moisture source, classically an ocean or large lake
  • Produces some of the highest precipitation totals in the world

Read the figure

  • Windward: rising air cools and condenses
  • Leeward: descending air warms and dries, creating a rain shadow

Keep this in mind for the Oregon map at the end of the lecture.

Hygroscopic cloud seeding

Key idea

Cloud seeding adds particles to clouds to induce rainfall, a practice used to combat prolonged drought.

How it works (top panels)

1. Rain forms when vapor condenses on natural nuclei into small droplets

2. Droplets grow by collision–coalescence, but only once they reach about 20–30 microns

3. Hygroscopic flares burned at the cloud base release extra nuclei into the updraft, producing larger droplets

4. Droplets that reach about 1 mm are heavy enough to fall as rain

Delivery

By aircraft (silver iodide, bottom left), or by rockets fired from the ground (bottom right). Used since the 1940s.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q6 List the four conditions needed for precipitation to form.

1) The atmosphere becomes saturated (air lifted and cooled), 2) condensation nuclei are present, 3) particles collide to form droplets, 4) a constant supply of warm, moist air.

Q7 Match each lifting mechanism to an example: the ITCZ, a summer afternoon over a plowed field, the Cascades, a cold front over the Great Plains.

ITCZ: convergent. Plowed field: convection. Cascades: orographic. Cold front: frontal.

Q8 Why is the leeward side of a mountain range drier than the windward side?

Air rising on the windward side cools and drops its moisture. Air descending on the leeward side warms and dries: a rain shadow.

Part 4

Where precipitation falls

Global water vapor and precipitation patterns, and why western Oregon is so wet

Atmospheric water vapor

Key idea

Precipitable water is the total water content of a vertical column of atmosphere: all the water hanging over your head.

Read the maps

  • Left: January (Northern Hemisphere winter). Right: July (summer)
  • Darker blue = more precipitable water (5 to 40+ mm)

What to notice

  • The wettest air sits over the tropics
  • The moist band shifts north in the northern summer, following the sun

Mean annual global precipitation

Key idea

Precipitation is spread very unevenly across the globe.

What to notice

  • Precipitation is concentrated in the equatorial band (the ITCZ from the convergent lifting slide)
  • Large desert regions, such as the Sahara, Arabian Peninsula and central Australia, receive very little

Note on the legend

The legend is labeled probability percentage, so the colors are not rainfall depths. Read the pattern, not the values.

Compare it with the water vapor maps on the previous slide.

Mean annual precipitation in the U.S. and Oregon

Key idea

In both maps, the western side receives far more precipitation than the eastern side. Can you guess why?

Read the maps

  • U.S.: the wettest areas are the Pacific Northwest coast and the Southeast; the interior West is dry
  • Oregon: totals are highest along the coast and the Cascades, and much lower east of the Cascades on the Columbia Plateau

Think about it

Which lifting mechanism from Part 3 explains this pattern? Write down your answer, then check Q9.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q9 Why does the western side of Oregon receive so much more precipitation than the eastern side?

Orographic lifting: moist Pacific air is forced up the Coast Range and Cascades, cools and drops its moisture on the windward (west) side. Eastern Oregon lies in the rain shadow.

Q10 Where on Earth is precipitable water highest, and how does that band move through the year?

Over the tropics. The band shifts north in the northern summer (July) and south in the northern winter (January), following the sun.
